title: Hear the Driver

source.quote: The five drivers are the functional manifestations of not-OK (structural) counterscripts.

setting: Tuesday, 2:45pm. Weekly status round. Dana leads a small product team and has learned to watch the half-second before people answer, not just the answer.

L1.line: The deliverable is - and I want to be precise here - ninety, or really ninety-two percent complete.
cues: ticks the percentage off on two fingers
eyes flick up and to the side mid-sentence, like she's reading something off the ceiling
L1.question: Quick primer: a 'driver' is a lightning-fast pattern - half a second, in tone, word choice, and gesture - that shows up right before someone answers, like they're unconsciously proving an old rule such as 'I'm only OK if I'm perfect' or 'I'm only OK if I hurry.' Which driver is Lucia showing?

options.feedback: Try Hard sounds strangled and hunched, full of 'huh?' and 'what?' and 'it's hard to...'. Lucia's voice is smooth and her correction adds precision - that's not straining, that's something else.
Right. The self-correcting parenthesis ('ninety, or really ninety-two'), the finger count, and the eyes checking an invisible ceiling for the exact right number are the classic Be Perfect tells.
Hurry Up sounds staccato and rushed, with foot-tapping urgency. Lucia is actually slowing down to get the number exactly right - the opposite energy.
Be Strong shows up as flat, distancing, and gesture-free - 'that's done' instead of 'I did that.' Lucia is animated and precise, not withdrawn.

L1.lesson: Each driver has a distinct half-second signature in words, tone, gesture, and face. Be Perfect's tell is the self-correcting parenthesis plus the upward glance - as if the exact right number were written on the ceiling.

L2.intro: Two teammates, two different drivers, same afternoon. What Dana says in the next half-second either feeds the driver or offers its allower.

beats.line: Is this OK? I mean - it's probably fine, whatever works for you, really, sorry to even ask-
cues: eyebrows raised, head tilted down then glancing up
voice rising at the end of each clause

options.text: It's fine, don't worry about it!
options.outcome: Omar relaxes for a second, then immediately asks another small permission-seeking question about something else entirely.
options.lesson: Reassurance feels kind but doesn't touch the driver itself. Please Others runs on needing you to be pleased, so blanket reassurance just resets the loop instead of interrupting it.

options.text: Just make the call that makes me happy, I trust you.
options.outcome: Omar laughs a beat too quickly. 'Okay! Whatever you think is best, then!' - more pleasing, not less.
options.lesson: This answers his literal question - what will please you - instead of crossing it. It's complementary to his Please Others opening, so it reinforces the exact pattern it seems to be joking about.

options.text: What do you think is right here? Tell me that first.
options.outcome: A pause. Omar actually thinks about it, then gives a real opinion - a little shaky, but his own.
options.lesson: This is the allower underneath Please Others - 'please yourself' - turned into a concrete question instead of advice. It asks for his Adult instead of accepting the Child's offer.

options.text: You need to stop apologizing for every little thing, it's not professional.
options.outcome: Omar's shoulders rise further. 'Sorry - I mean - right, sorry.' The apology about the apologizing is still an apology.
options.lesson: Naming the pattern from Parent judgment just gives his Adapted Child one more thing to try to please you about. The fix isn't a correction - it's an invitation to his own Adult.

beats.line: Quick, quick - just send it, we don't have time for this, go go go.
cues: rapid-fire delivery, words almost running together
eyes darting to the clock and back

options.text: You're right, let's just send it now.
options.outcome: They send it. Ten minutes later they catch an error a thirty-second check would've caught.
options.lesson: Matching someone's Hurry Up is complementary, not helpful - it feels productive in the moment and reliably produces exactly the rework Hurry Up scripts predict.

options.text: Take thirty seconds. I'll time it.
options.outcome: Caleb exhales, actually re-reads it, and catches the error himself. 'Oh - good thing we checked.'
options.lesson: 'Take your time' as a vague instruction doesn't land on someone mid-driver. Turning it into a small, bounded, concrete action does.

options.outcome: Caleb nods, but his foot keeps tapping. He sends it two minutes later anyway, barely slower than before.
options.lesson: Telling someone to relax rarely works mid-driver - the allower has to be a specific action, not a mood you're asking them to adopt.

options.text: We're always behind because of you.
options.outcome: Caleb's typing gets even faster and more frantic.
options.lesson: Blame adds stress on top of a stress-behavior - it's the fastest way to deepen someone's Hurry Up, not interrupt it.

fields.label: The second Caleb's fix is confirmed, Dana's pen is already tapping the next line on the agenda - she hasn't actually looked at his screen yet. Name the driver she just caught herself running, and the one specific tell that gave it away.
Write the allower Dana could give herself in that exact second, the same kind she offered Omar and Caleb - something she could actually do, not just a feeling to adopt.

echo.setting: Saturday, the gym. Dana's trainer, mid-set, breathing hard.
echo.line: 'I'm fine, keep going' - said flat, immobile face, arms already back in position before anyone asked if he was actually fine.
